title: Exponential burst buffer + observer telemetry playbook for fair limiter recovery
creator: Priya Shah
description:
Problem statement: We observe occasional short-lived traffic spikes that cause limiter state thrashing (cold starts of token leases, disproportionate tenant eviction, and increased tail latency). In multi-region traffic surges, failing over to a secondary region can cause cascading re-admissions that further destabilize quotas. Existing mitigation strategies (static burst allowances and hard circuit breakers) either allow unfair token capture by aggressive tenants or cause excessive error rates for latency-sensitive traffic.

Goal: Implement an "exponential burst buffer" admission layer paired with an "observer telemetry" surface to (1) absorb short spikes without changing long-term quotas, (2) preserve proportional fairness across tenants during transient overloads, (3) provide an operable circuit-breaker fallback for limiter outages, and (4) enable measurable SLO trade-offs with dashboards and runbooks.

Design summary:
- Exponential burst buffer (ebb): a per-region, in-memory short-term buffer that accepts a small, time-decaying extra credit for each tenant. Credits decay exponentially (configurable half-life) so bursts are absorbed for a bounded window without permanent quota transfer. The buffer is sized by region and tenant tier, with strict global caps.
- Probabilistic admission gating: when region limiter saturation is reached, ebb performs probabilistic acceptance weighted by tenant priority and recent successful request ratio to avoid deterministic starvation.
- Observer telemetry: compute a fairness_index metric per tenant cohort (0.0..1.0) derived from achieved share vs. expected share over sliding windows; expose percentile of fairness_index and a tenant-skew score. Track burst-absorbed-tokens and decay_curve_slopes as metrics.
- Circuit and regional failover policy: on limiter backend outage or sustained saturation, engage a staged circuit: (a) short soft-fallback to detector-owned standby (local queueing + limited retry), (b) region steer to next-best region with capacity-aware routing, (c) global degradation mode honoring SLO-derived priorities. Each stage emits structured events to the console and triggers runbook pages.
- Rollback and safety: conservative default configs, kill-switch feature flag, and gradual rollout to a subset of tenants. Canary monitors: error budget burn rate, fairness_index delta, and 99th-token-latency.

Implementation plan (milestones):
1) Simulation harness (2w): extend existing limiter simulator to model ebb credits, decay rates, probabilistic admission, and multi-region failover. Run tenant-mix scenarios (PLG-heavy, enterprise-heavy, mixed) and produce fairness/latency/cost trade-off curves.
2) Telemetry schema (1w): define metrics and tracing spans; add tags for tenant_id, cohort, region, admission_path (limiter|ebb|prob-pass|prob-drop), and decision_token. Wire to console dashboards and alerting rules.
3) Runtime prototype (3w): implement ebb as a lightweight in-process layer with backing state in memory and optional persistent checkpoints for graceful restart. Add admission policy engine and per-tenant caps.
4) Canary rollout (2w): deploy to single region, opt-in small tenant subset. Monitor fairness_index, request error rate, and token consumption. Perform live chaos tests (throttle limiter, inject latency, simulate regional failover).
5) Global rollout + playbook (1w): when canary stable, expand configuration and publish a runbook with operational procedures for recovery and manual overrides.

Trade-offs and reasoning:
- Ebb vs large static bursts: a time-decaying buffer limits long-term quota drift while providing quick absorption. Static large bursts are simpler but favor aggressive tenants and make SLO accounting harder.
- In-process buffer vs central ledger: in-process is lower latency and simpler for short windows; we accept increased complexity in crash recovery and provide lightweight checkpointing instead of a heavy consensus-backed ledger.
- Probabilistic admission introduces non-determinism which can complicate reproducibility; mitigated by deterministic sampling seeds per-window in debug mode and detailed traces.

Observability and SLOs:
- New metrics: fairness_index, ebb_absorbed_tokens, ebb_rejection_rate, prob_accept_rate, regional_failover_count.
- Dashboards: per-tenant cohort fairness trend, regional heatmap of ebb consumption, SLO burn charts annotated with ebb-engaged periods.
- Alerts: fairness_index < 0.5 for >5m, ebb_rejection_rate > 2% sustained for 3m, staged increase in error-budget-burn during canary.

Runbook excerpts (to be expanded in playbook):
- On fairness regression: pause ebb for offender cohorts, increase decay rate by 2x, and re-run simulated admission traces.
- On regional limiter outage: engage staged circuit for 30s, failover to nearest region if throughput cannot be restored, and notify platform on-call.
- On unexpected high ebb usage: flip kill-switch and fall back to default limiter behavior; immediately run fairness metrics and contact product owner.

Links and artifacts:
- Design doc (draft): https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Exponential+Burst+Buffer+Design
- Simulator PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/limiter-sim/pull/314
- Early dashboard (Grafana): https://grafana.redwood.ai/d/limiter/ebb-playbook
- Canary runbook doc: https://confluence.redwood.ai/display/INF/Ebb+Canary+Runbook

Success criteria:
- No more than 10% relative increase in 99th-token-latency in canary tenants during typical spikes.
- fairness_index median across cohorts remains within 5% of baseline during bursts.
- Canaries show <1% additional error budget burn attributable to ebb admission logic.

Next steps:
- Finish simulator scenarios and upload result CSVs to the design doc (target 2026-03-12).
- Prototype ebb admission engine and land PR for internal review (target 2026-03-24).
- Schedule cross-team review with Console and Product for dashboard coverage and SLA wording (invite sent).
